title: A privacy order can create vehicle-data control rights without proving that consumers can use them
source_unit: Federal Trade Commission final order and complaint concerning GM and OnStar connected-vehicle geolocation and driving-behavior data practices; named firm-level enforcement record, not a representative consumer sample
geography: United States federal consumer-protection enforcement and GM/OnStar connected-vehicle customers

observations.period: January 2026; FTC final order and complaint

data_copy_request.value: required process for U.S. consumers to request a copy of connected-vehicle data

data_deletion_request.value: required process for U.S. consumers to seek deletion of connected-vehicle data

collection_disable.value: required ability to disable precise geolocation collection where vehicle technology permits

data_collection_opt_out.value: required opt-out route for collection of geolocation and driving-behavior data, subject to stated exceptions

consumer_use_and_effectiveness.unit: missing request volume, approval, completion, deletion verification, residual data, downstream use, trust, switching, or vehicle-mobility outcome

observations.method: FTC official complaint and finalized-order review; the order's duration, required control surfaces, and stated exceptions are coded separately from actual consumer use or implementation success.
observations.uncertainty: The order establishes firm obligations and available control routes, not the number of affected consumers, the number who requested access or deletion, the response time, the completeness of deletion, the operation of disable/opt-out controls, or later consumer trust and behavior.
observations.subgroup: U.S. connected-vehicle customers, including customers whose vehicle technology supports disabling collection; data categories and exceptions remain governed by the order's terms.
observations.counterinterpretation: A formal access, deletion, disable, or opt-out route may materially improve contestability for some customers while remaining difficult to find, understand, request, verify, or use without losing valued vehicle services. A privacy order is not automatically a restored privacy outcome.

observations.period: June 17, 2026; GM U.S. Consumer Privacy Statement control and exit conditions

disconnect_residual_collection.unit: GM says geolocation and vehicle information may still be collected after OnStar unenrollment to restore connectivity or address high-voltage-battery overheating

privacy_service_tradeoff.unit: the statement describes emergency, safety, navigation, stolen-vehicle, and connected-service functions but does not measure what consumers lose when controls are used

third_party_and_transfer_surface.unit: dealer, affiliate, service-provider, vehicle-transfer, and third-party-service boundaries remain part of the control problem

observations.method: Review of the dated official GM U.S. Consumer Privacy Statement, including connected-vehicle controls, data categories, transfer/unenrollment language, model-year qualification, and safety exceptions; stated control conditions are kept separate from consumer attempts and verified outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The statement does not show which vehicles or users encountered the residual-collection exception, whether consumers understood the trade-off, whether privacy settings worked as intended, or whether a user switched vehicles, services, or providers.
observations.subgroup: GM/OnStar-connected-vehicle users; control availability varies by vehicle model/year, service enrollment, technology, state, and emergency or safety circumstance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Safety and emergency exceptions may protect occupants and vehicle systems rather than undermine privacy; the unresolved issue is whether consumers can understand and choose the boundary while retaining valued services.

observations.period: June 2026; GM U.S. Consumer Privacy Statement implementation route

request_channels.value: verifiable U.S. Consumer Privacy Request Form or phone; email requests not accepted

processing_window.value: up to 45 days in some cases

location_control.value: some model-year 2019 and later vehicles may disable OnStar location services through in-vehicle Privacy Settings

disconnect_route.value: phone advisor or in-vehicle blue button; stated emergency, safety, and battery-overheating exceptions remain

request_completion_and_effect.unit: missing request attempt, identity verification, response, deletion, residual collection, service effect, trust, or switching outcome

observations.method: Current GM U.S. Consumer Privacy Statement review; route channel, response timing, vehicle-technology eligibility, unenrollment exceptions, and unobserved completion are coded separately.
observations.uncertainty: The statement describes available routes and firm policy, not actual consumer request volume, identity-verification burden, approval, completion, deletion verification, model-level coverage, or whether using a control changes valued safety or service functions.
observations.subgroup: GM/OnStar consumers covered by the U.S. statement; location-control availability varies by vehicle technology and model year, while legal rights vary by residence.
observations.counterinterpretation: A published form, phone route, or in-vehicle setting can make a right more reachable, but a 45-day window, verification, model eligibility, phone dependence, exceptions, or valued service trade-offs can still leave practical control unequal.

related_sources.claim: FTC case materials identify the GM and OnStar enforcement matter and its order record.
FTC describes the allegations, final order, and required consumer data-control routes.
GM describes U.S. request channels, stated processing timing, model-dependent location controls, unenrollment routes, and continuing safety/emergency exceptions.

boundary: This record adds a named privacy and connected-vehicle data-governance remedy to the platform/data and consumer-power atlas. It establishes a formal firm response and possible control surfaces, not actual data access, deletion, disabling, opt-out completion, deletion verification, reduced exposure, restored trust, switching, or mobility benefit. The next test is an authorized implementation record preserving request, response, completion, verification, service trade-off, and later use or exit separately.
